chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Fractional Real Estate Ownership Actually Is

lessons.title: The Ticket-Size Problem in Indian Real Estate

children.text: A 42-year-old IT manager in Bengaluru has built a solid mutual fund and stock portfolio through Zerodha over the past decade. She wants to add commercial real estate for the steady rental income and diversification it offers, income that historically does not move in step with the Nifty. She calls a broker about buying a floor in an upcoming Grade-A office tower on the Outer Ring Road. The quote comes back at ₹52 crore. She closes the browser tab. This is not a story about one investor. It is the reason an entire industry of fractional ownership platforms exists.

body.text: Institutional-grade commercial real estate in India has always delivered stable, bond-like rental income. The problem was never the asset class. It was the ticket size, which kept it locked away from everyone except large institutions, family offices and the ultra-wealthy.

children.text: Why Investors Want a Slice of Commercial Real Estate

behaves differently from a stock portfolio. Rents are contracted for three to nine years, tenants are usually large corporates or MNCs on long leases, and income arrives every month regardless of what the market is doing that day. For an HNI or an experienced retail investor already holding equity and mutual funds, this is the appeal: a return stream that does not move in lockstep with the Sensex or Nifty.

children.text: The Wall Every Retail Investor Hits: Ticket Size

The yields above look attractive on a spreadsheet. The problem shows up the moment you try to actually buy the asset. A single floor in an institutional-grade office tower, the kind occupied by a large corporate tenant on a nine-year lease, is not sold for ₹20 lakh or even ₹2 crore. It is sold for tens of crores, because the building is not divisible in any legal or practical sense. You either buy the whole floor, or you do not buy it at all.

body.title: How much of the building do you actually own?
body.prompt: A Grade-A office building in Gurugram is valued at ₹120 crore. Through a fractional ownership platform, an investor commits ₹30 lakh to the SPV that owns this building. What percentage of the building does this investor own?
body.explanation: ₹30 lakh ÷ ₹120 crore = 0.25%. Against the ₹52 crore floor purchase from the opening example, that same ₹30 lakh would work out to roughly 0.058% and would not even be a transaction most direct sellers are set up to handle, since whole-floor sales do not usually sell in fractions at all. Closing that gap is exactly what fractional structures exist to do.

body.text: This is why, for decades, institutional-grade Indian commercial real estate was owned almost entirely by insurance companies, pension funds, family offices and a small number of ultra-wealthy individuals. It was never that retail investors did not want the asset class. They simply could not write a cheque large enough to get in the door.

children.text: What Investors Tried Before Platforms Existed

Retail investors did not sit still. The common workaround was informal: a group of friends, relatives or colleagues pooling money to jointly buy a property, with an understanding, rarely a proper legal agreement, on how rent and any eventual sale proceeds would be split.

body.text: Informal joint ownership of real estate in India tends to create problems that surface exactly when you do not want them to. Title is usually registered in the name of one or two people, not all investors, which leaves the rest holding nothing more than a private promise. There is no defined exit: if one investor wants out, the whole property has to be sold, and every other investor has to agree to it. Disputes over shared maintenance costs, tenant selection and rent collection are common, and by the time one reaches court, the friendship and the investment both tend to be losses.

children.text: Where REITs and Fractional Platforms Fit In

Two structures now exist to close this gap, and the rest of this course is built around them. Listed REITs let you buy a tiny, tradeable slice of a large, diversified portfolio through your demat account, the same way you would buy a share on NSE. Fractional ownership platforms, and the SM REITs that now regulate a large part of that space, let you co-own one specific property through an SPV, alongside other investors, at a ticket size measured in lakhs instead of crores.

body.label: SEBI's minimum ticket size for SM REITs
body.context: Set under SEBI's Small and Medium REIT (SM REIT) Regulations, notified in 2024. That is roughly 1/500th of the ₹52 crore quote for a single office floor in the opening example. Chapter 2 covers this framework in full.

body.title: Show me the cap rate math

children.text: Cap rate math is what ties a building's rental income directly to its price, and it explains why a well-tenanted office tower ends up costing so much.
is the annual rent collected, minus operating costs like maintenance, property tax and insurance, before any loan interest.

markDefs.definition: Annual rental income minus operating expenses such as maintenance, property tax and insurance. It excludes loan interest and depreciation.

content.caption: The same formula sellers use to justify a building's asking price

children.text: Take a hypothetical Grade-A office building generating ₹8 crore in NOI for the year. At a cap rate of 8%, roughly the middle of the typical range for such assets, the implied value works out to ₹8 crore ÷ 0.08 = ₹100 crore.

Push the cap rate down to 7%, meaning investors accept a lower yield for what they see as a safer asset, and the same ₹8 crore of NOI implies a value of ₹114.3 crore. Rent has not changed by a rupee. The price moved purely because buyers were willing to accept less income per rupee invested. This is why large, well-leased buildings carry such high price tags even when the underlying rent looks unremarkable on its own.

body.title: ₹25 lakh, no interest in managing a property
body.scenario: You have ₹25 lakh you want to allocate to commercial real estate, kept separate from your equity and mutual fund portfolio. You are not interested in day-to-day property management, chasing tenants or handling maintenance calls.
body.prompt: Based on this lesson, name at least two routes that are actually open to you at this ticket size, and one that is not.
body.modelAnswer: Open to you: a listed REIT (buy units through your demat account, any amount from the price of one unit upward) and an SM REIT or a fractional ownership platform (both typically need a minimum around ₹10 lakh, so ₹25 lakh clears that bar). Not open to you: direct ownership of a Grade-A office floor or building, which typically needs tens of crores. ₹25 lakh would not cover even the stamp duty and registration on a large commercial asset in most Indian cities, let alone the purchase price itself.

points: Institutional-grade Indian commercial real estate has always offered stable, bond-like yields; the barrier was never the returns, it was the ticket size.
A single floor in a Grade-A office tower typically costs tens of crores because the building cannot be legally or practically subdivided.
Cap rate math means the same rental income can imply very different property values depending on what yield buyers are willing to accept.
Informal joint ownership among friends or family fixes the ticket-size problem on paper but usually fails on title, exit and dispute resolution.
Listed REITs and SM REITs/fractional platforms exist specifically to close this gap, at ticket sizes measured in lakhs rather than crores.
SEBI's SM REIT framework sets a ₹10 lakh minimum investment, which the rest of this course treats as the entry point into this asset class.
